 Rules for Choosing a 4 -Bay NAS
 1 Start with 3 equal drives under SHR / RAID 5 to enjoy 1-drive parity while leaving 1 bay free for zero-downtime future expansion. 
 2 Use RAID 5 for media and backups to maximize capacity (75% usable). Choose RAID 6 / SHR-2 dual parity for irreplaceable business files. 
 3 If streaming 4K movies with subtitle transcoding, verify that the NAS processor features an Intel Quick Sync GPU. 
 4 Pair 4-bay systems with a compatible UPS (Uninterruptible Power Supply) to prevent array corruption during unexpected power outages. 
 Mistakes to Avoid Before Buying
 ✕ Filling all 4 bays on day 1 with small 2TB drives, eliminating easy expansion. 
 ✕ Choosing a non-iGPU processor (like AMD Ryzen V1500B) when intensive 4K Plex hardware transcoding is required. 
 ✕ Overlooking noise: 4 × 7200rpm drives can be audible in a bedroom; locate the NAS in an office or utility closet. 
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Why is a 4-bay NAS considered the best choice for home use?
 A 4-bay NAS hits the mathematical sweet spot: RAID 5 gives you 75% usable capacity (versus 50% in a 2-bay RAID 1 mirror), while providing full 1-disk failure protection. You can also populate 3 bays initially and preserve the 4th bay for hassle-free storage expansion.
 What is the cheapest 4-bay NAS in 2026?
 Enclosures like the TerraMaster F4-424 and UGREEN DXP4800 represent the most affordable modern 4-bay entry points with Intel processors, starting around $400 to $450 before hard drives.
 How much does a complete 4-bay NAS cost with hard drives?
 Use the exact-model cost table below the picks and compare both total spend and protected capacity. Three 12TB drives under single parity provide 24TB decimal capacity; four provide 36TB. Checkout prices, tax, shipping, backup storage, and network upgrades can change the final budget.
 Can I start a 4-bay NAS with just 2 hard drives?
 Some systems allow a two-drive mirror or SHR pool to grow by adding disks and migrating to single parity. The supported steps depend on the operating system and existing RAID layout; conversion is not automatic on every NAS. Read the model-specific procedure and verify your independent backup before changing the pool.
 What is the difference between RAID 5 and RAID 6 in a 4-bay NAS?
 RAID 5 allocates one drive worth of storage to parity (75% usable with 4 drives) and survives one disk failure. RAID 6 uses dual parity (50% usable with 4 drives) and survives two simultaneous drive crashes, which is recommended for mission-critical business retention or when rebuilding high-capacity 16TB+ arrays.

 Check price on Amazon ↗ 
 Your NAS has two empty M.2 slots. The tempting move is to fill them, click Cache and expect everything to fly. The better move is to ask what you want to feel faster: the apps you run, repeated reads from hard drives, or a workload waiting for durable writes.
 For a small homelab, start with an SSD pool for apps and VMs. Choose Samsung 990 PRO 2TB for that job, WD Red SN700 2TB for a NAS-focused drive, SN700 4TB for more capacity and total write endurance, or Crucial T500 1TB for a smaller project with onboard DRAM. Buy cache only when you can name the bottleneck.
 Specs come from the makers; pool and cache guidance comes from the NAS and ZFS documentation. 
 Need more M.2 sockets for those SSDs? Our NVMe PCIe expansion-card guide compares host bifurcation with an onboard PCIe switch, including the slot map that determines which drives appear.
 Quick picks: give each SSD a job
 Best app/VM pool: Samsung 990 PRO 2TB. TLC flash, 2GB of LPDDR4 and a PCIe 4.0 interface make it a sensible starting point for active application storage on a compatible host. Use a matching pair when you want a mirrored pool.
 Best NAS-branded: WD Red SN700 2TB. Its published 2,500TBW rating and NAS-focused design are the attraction. Pick it for the workload and compatibility, rather than chasing a newer PCIe generation.
 Best total endurance: WD Red SN700 4TB. The 5,100TBW rating is the largest in this shortlist, alongside twice the capacity of the 2TB models. That makes it useful for a larger active-data pool with sustained writes.
 Best for a smaller pool: Crucial T500 1TB. Keep TLC and onboard DRAM while buying the capacity your app collection needs. Leave room for VM disks, databases and snapshots to grow.
 The parts lists offer alternatives. Choose the model and capacity for your pool; you don’t need all four drives.
 App pool, read cache or SLOG?
 These names describe different jobs. Pick the job before the SSD.
 What you want to improve 
 Start here 
 What the SSD does 
 App data, VM disks and frequently used project files 
 A separate SSD data pool 
 Stores the active data directly 
 Repeated random reads that miss the RAM cache 
 Investigate L2ARC after sizing RAM 
 Keeps a second copy of selected read data 
 Latency from synchronous writes 
 Investigate a suitable SLOG device 
 Holds the separate intent log for durable-write acknowledgements 
 A large, mostly sequential file copy 
 Find the storage or network limit first 
 Extra cache may leave the actual bottleneck untouched 
 SLOG and L2ARC rarely belong at the top of a small homelab’s shopping list. An SSD pool for apps and VMs is often the more useful upgrade: you decide exactly which data lives on it. TrueNAS’s ZFS primer explicitly describes separate SSD and HDD pools as a potentially more efficient layout for active and rarely used data.
 Keep the bulk files on hard drives and put the busy application data on SSDs. Our NAS-drive guide covers the capacity tier; the RAID, snapshots and backups guide covers protecting both tiers.
 Compare capacity and write endurance

 Equivalent full-drive writes = published TBW divided by the advertised decimal capacity in TB. This compares the write allowance across capacities; it doesn’t predict a failure date. 
 The 4TB SN700’s bigger total allowance comes largely with its bigger capacity. Per TB of storage, the two SN700 models are close. Choose 4TB because you need the room and total write budget, rather than expecting a dramatic change in endurance per TB.
 All four models have a five-year limited warranty ; the makers’ endurance and warranty conditions still apply. Samsung and Crucial specify time or TBW, whichever comes first. Read the Samsung 990 PRO datasheet , WD Red SN700 product brief and Micron’s T500 product flyer for the capacity-specific figures.
 First: does your NAS accept the drive for this job?
 Synology: the model and DSM rules come first
 The DS225+ has no M.2 slots , so skip an NVMe purchase for that box. Our UGREEN DXP2800 vs Synology DS225+ comparison covers the expansion differences; the DS225+ datasheet lists its SATA drive support.
 For an M.2-equipped Synology, separate cache support from M.2 storage-pool support . Synology’s 2025-and-later drive policy gives DSM 7.3 more flexibility with third-party HDDs and 2.5-inch SATA SSDs. M.2 NVMe still has its own compatibility requirements for new pools and caches.
 The official M.2 pool requirements say to use compatible Synology M.2 SSDs on supported models. Start with the compatibility list for your exact NAS and DSM version. This consumer-drive shortlist is aimed at compatible open-platform hosts and NAS configurations, rather than a blanket Synology upgrade list.
 UGREEN: two slots, two possible roles
 UGREEN lists two M.2 SSD slots on both the DXP2800 and DXP4800 Plus . The DXP4800 Plus documentation describes using its NVMe slots for cache or a dedicated SSD storage pool, including containers and VMs.
 Choose the role in the NAS storage software, then follow that model’s drive and installation guidance. A pair reserved for an app pool is a different layout from a pair assigned to HDD cache. Plan the layout before moving data, and keep a backup ready for a pool change.
 For a DIY NAS, M.2 uses the motherboard or an appropriate PCIe adapter. A SATA expansion card won’t create an NVMe connection; our SATA/HBA guide explains the separate SATA/SAS side of the build.
 Why an app pool is usually the happier first upgrade
 Containers, VM images and active project directories give you a clear destination for the SSDs. Put those datasets on the SSD pool and leave the big media/archive collection on HDDs. You can then judge the upgrade with the app or VM you actually use.
 For important active data, a mirrored pair gives you drive-failure redundancy. It still needs snapshots and a separate backup. Decide how much usable capacity the project needs before filling both M.2 slots with the smallest drives you can find.
 The 990 PRO 2TB is the default app-pool pick for its capacity, TLC and explicitly documented DRAM. The T500 1TB is the smaller alternative when your active data fits comfortably. The SN700 models put more emphasis on the published write allowance. Those are useful buying differences without turning a desktop benchmark into a NAS result.
 Boot storage is another job again. Keep it separate from app-pool planning where your platform requires that; our NVMe boot-drive guide covers choosing a system drive.
 L2ARC: help RAM, don’t try to replace it
 ZFS already uses RAM as its first read cache, ARC . L2ARC adds a second read-cache tier on an SSD. It earns its place when frequently reused data misses ARC and enough of that working set can fit on the SSD.
 TrueNAS’s L2ARC explanation describes that overflow role. Its ZFS primer also explains that L2ARC consumes RAM for tracking data. Give the system enough memory first, then inspect cache behavior for your actual workload.
 If your NAS mainly serves a film once or receives a long backup stream, start by investigating the workload and network path. Buying a large cache SSD won’t make every transfer faster. If the slow bit is an app’s active dataset, putting that dataset on an SSD pool is the simpler plan.
 SLOG: buy power-loss protection, not a gaming badge
 A SLOG handles the separate intent log for synchronous writes . It isn’t a general write cache, and it doesn’t turn an HDD pool into an SSD pool. TrueNAS’s SLOG guide explains how the log lets ZFS acknowledge synchronous transactions on non-volatile storage.
 For this job, choose a low-latency device with documented in-flight power-loss protection (PLP) . OpenZFS’s cache and log guide distinguishes SLOG from asynchronous writes and calls for power-loss protection.
 None of the four picks here is our SLOG recommendation. Use them for their app-pool or suitable cache role. If measurements show a synchronous-write bottleneck, shop for an explicitly qualified PLP device instead. A UPS helps with outages, but it doesn’t add PLP circuitry to an SSD.
 DRAM, HMB and heat: three different fit checks
 Onboard DRAM is memory on the SSD for its controller. It is separate from the NAS’s RAM and ZFS ARC. Samsung explicitly lists the 990 PRO’s DRAM; Micron’s T500 model guide specifies LPDDR4 at 1GB per 1TB of NAND.
 Host Memory Buffer (HMB) uses part of the host’s memory for SSD flash management, as explained in Kioxia’s HMB technical brief . Don’t confuse that with onboard DRAM or a NAS read-cache tier. WD’s cited SN700 brief leaves DRAM/HMB unspecified, so its recommendation rests on its documented NAS role and endurance.
 Cooling and physical fit matter too. All four picks are M.2 2280 NVMe drives. The selected 990 PRO and T500 variants are the versions without a tall factory heatsink. Use the NAS’s specified thermal pads and covers, keep its airflow clear, and match the SSD/heatsink height to the slot clearance. A heatsink built for a roomy desktop or console can be the wrong shape under a NAS cover.
 Make the upgrade earn its slots
 Back up the app data, power down before installing M.2 drives, and follow the host’s instructions to create the intended pool or cache. For an app pool, move the relevant datasets and app storage deliberately. Then test the app, check drive health and temperatures during use, and verify a restore of something you care about.
 990 PRO 2TB for an app/VM pool. SN700 2TB for the NAS-focused choice. SN700 4TB for more room and total write endurance. T500 1TB for the smaller project with DRAM. Pick the job, buy the capacity, and save the clever cache experiment for a bottleneck you’ve actually found.

 Quick Summary (TL;DR): 
The best NVMe SSD for a NAS is not necessarily the drive with the highest desktop benchmark. For cache , prioritise endurance, steady-state random I/O, thermals and power-loss behaviour. For Docker, VMs and application pools , capacity and predictable latency matter more. Our best all-round NAS -oriented choice is the WD Red SN700 : M.2 2280, PCIe 3.0 x4, capacities from 250GB to 4TB, a 5-year warranty and endurance up to 5,100TBW on the 4TB model. The Seagate IronWolf 525 is another strong NAS -focused option with PCIe 4.0 x4, 500GB–2TB capacities, 5-year warranty and up to 2,800TBW on the 2TB model, with published sustained-write figures rather than only fresh-out-of-box bursts. For supported Synology systems, the SNV5420 is the safest compatibility-first choice: M.2 2280, PCIe 3.0 x4, enterprise workload endurance, 5-year warranty and built-in power-loss protection . The Kingston DC2000B is excellent for compact high-integrity cache/server use, with M.2 2280, hardware PLP, 0.4 DWPD endurance and capacities up to 960GB. The Samsung 990 PRO is the performance/capacity choice for container and VM pools, with 1–4TB capacity and up to 2,400TBW at 4TB, but it is a consumer SSD without the enterprise PLP emphasis of Synology/Kingston. Before buying, verify your NAS ’s exact M.2 function, supported SSD list, maximum capacity, PCIe lane width and heatsink clearance. A 7GB/s SSD in a PCIe 3.0 x1 NAS slot will still perform like an x1 device.
 Best NVMe SSDs for NAS Cache and Containers: Shortlist
 SSD Interface Capacity Endurance highlight Best for 
 WD Red SN700 PCIe 3.0 x4 250GB–4TB Up to 5,100TBW Best all-round NAS cache / app pool 
 Seagate IronWolf 525 PCIe 4.0 x4 500GB–2TB Up to 2,800TBW High-endurance NAS workloads 
 Synology SNV5420 PCIe 3.0 x4 400GB–1.6TB >700–2,900TBW + PLP Supported Synology cache/pools 
 Kingston DC2000B PCIe 4.0 x4 240GB–960GB 0.4 DWPD / 5 years + PLP Enterprise-style cache / server apps 
 Samsung 990 PRO PCIe 4.0 x4 1TB–4TB 600–2,400TBW Containers, VMs, high-capacity flash pool 
 Start with the NAS Slot, Not the SSD Benchmark
 An SSD can only run as fast as the slot that connects it.
 M.2 NVMe slots in NAS systems vary dramatically:
 PCIe 3.0 x1.
 PCIe 3.0 x2.
 PCIe 3.0 x4.
 PCIe 4.0 x1/x2/x4.
 Shared lanes between two M.2 slots.
 A PCIe 3.0 lane provides roughly 1GB/s-class interconnect bandwidth per direction. So a PCIe 3.0 x1 NAS slot cannot expose the 7GB/s sequential specification of a flagship PCIe 4.0 x4 desktop SSD.
 The Network Can Be the Bottleneck Too
 Network Raw line-rate equivalent 
 1GbE 125MB/s 
 2.5GbE 312.5MB/s 
 5GbE 625MB/s 
 10GbE 1,250MB/s 
 NVMe still helps internal workloads such as containers, VMs and databases even when client networking is slower. But do not buy a top-end SSD expecting a single 2.5GbE SMB client to see multi-gigabyte-per-second transfers.
 Cache and Container Storage Need Different SSD Priorities
 For cache, prioritise:
 Write endurance.
 Steady-state random I/O.
 Power-loss protection for write cache where required.
 Thermal consistency.
 Vendor compatibility.
 For containers / VM pools, prioritise:
 Capacity.
 Low random latency.
 Reasonable endurance.
 RAID/mirroring support.
 Price per usable flash TB.
 Our architecture guide explains when you should use cache at all: NAS NVMe Cache vs SSD Storage Pool: Which Should You Use? .
 Best All-Round NAS NVMe: WD Red SN700
 The WD Red SN700 is designed specifically around NAS workloads rather than gaming/desktop peak speed.
 M.2 2280.

 For a home NAS that may write constantly to cache or run databases and containers 24/7, this endurance is more relevant than whether the SSD can hit 7GB/s for a short desktop benchmark.
 Where SN700 Fits Best

 Docker and application pools.
 VM storage.

 Its PCIe 3.0 x4 interface is also a good match for many NAS M.2 slots; paying for a PCIe 5.0 SSD would often provide no useful advantage.
 Best Alternative NAS-Focused SSD: Seagate IronWolf 525
 The IronWolf 525 is Seagate’s current NAS-focused NVMe family.

 Best Synology Compatibility Choice: SNV5420
 Synology’s current enterprise M.2 SSD family is expensive compared with consumer SSDs, but it exists for a reason: validated compatibility and controlled behaviour inside Synology systems.

 Why Power-Loss Protection Matters
 Hardware power-loss protection uses capacitors to give the SSD enough reserve energy to finish critical internal writes after input power disappears unexpectedly.
 It is especially valuable for:
 Write-back cache.
 Database storage.
 VM disks.
 Business-critical application pools.
 A UPS protects the NAS as a system, but PLP protects the SSD’s own internal mapping/write process during sudden power loss.
 Synology’s Compatibility Rules Can Make SNV5420 the Rational Choice
 Current Synology models distinguish M.2 cache support from M.2 storage-pool support, and supported M.2 storage pools are subject to Synology’s compatibility requirements.
 That means a cheaper third-party SSD may not be equivalent if DSM refuses the intended storage-pool configuration or support is restricted.
 Check the exact model in NAS Drive Compatibility: What to Check on Synology, UGREEN and QNAP .
 Best Compact Enterprise Cache SSD: Kingston DC2000B
 Kingston’s DC2000B is not marketed as a consumer NAS drive. It is a data-centre M.2 SSD designed for server boot and caching workloads.

 DC2000B Is About Consistency, Not Capacity

 It is much more interesting for:
 Read-write cache.
 Small database pools.
 Server boot/application storage.

 The 960GB model is rated at 700TBW and Kingston publishes steady-state random I/O figures rather than only burst results.
 Watch Heatsink Clearance with DC2000B
 Kingston sells heatsink and non-heatsink versions.
 The heatsink version is approximately 8.3mm high, while the bare module is about 3.5mm high.
 Many NAS M.2 compartments have tight clearance or their own thermal pad /heatsink. Verify physical fit before ordering the heatsink version.
 Best High-Capacity Container / VM Pool: Samsung 990 PRO
 The Samsung 990 PRO is a consumer/performance NVMe SSD, not a NAS-enterprise SSD.
 It can still be an excellent storage-pool choice when the NAS accepts it and the workload fits its endurance profile.

 Those numbers are strong for container/VM pools in a home lab, but they are lower per terabyte than drives specifically designed around heavy NAS caching such as SN700.
 Why We Prefer 990 PRO for Storage Pools Rather Than Heavy Write Cache
 For Docker/VM storage, you gain:
 Up to 4TB capacity.

 For constant write-back cache, however, we prefer a drive with stronger NAS/enterprise endurance positioning and hardware PLP where the platform/workload needs it.
 Do Not Pay for PCIe 4.0/5.0 Speed Your NAS Cannot Use
 A Samsung 990 PRO or IronWolf 525 can negotiate down to slower PCIe generations, but you still paid for a high-performance controller.
 If your NAS provides only PCIe 3.0 x1 or x2 per M.2 slot, an SN700-class drive can be a more rational match.
 Peak sequential speed should therefore be near the bottom of your NAS SSD buying criteria.
 M.2 2280 Compatibility Matters
 Most consumer/prosumer NAS systems use M.2 2280 slots.
 Enterprise SSD families may also come in 22110, E1.S or U.2/U.3 form factors that physically will not fit.

 Maximum supported capacity.
 Thermals Matter More Than Desktop Benchmarks Suggest
 A NAS can run NVMe drives continuously in a confined chassis.
 Cache and databases can create sustained writes for hours rather than the short desktop bursts seen in many reviews.
 When temperature rises too far, the SSD controller may throttle to protect itself.
 A theoretically slower drive that stays cool can outperform a flagship SSD that repeatedly throttles.
 Use the NAS Heatsink Where Provided
 Many NAS vendors supply thermal pads/heatsinks designed around their M.2 bay.
 Use them according to the vendor instructions.
 Do not stack a large desktop SSD heatsink into a space that is not designed for it.
 TBW Is Useful, but It Is Not the Whole Endurance Story
 TBW means terabytes written over the drive’s rated warranty/endurance life.
 It is useful for comparing similar drives, but also look at:
 DWPD.
 Warranty length.
 Steady-state write performance.
 NAND type.
 Over-provisioning.
 Power-loss protection.
 Operating temperature.
 DWPD Can Be Easier for Write-Cache Planning
 DWPD means drive writes per day.
 A 1TB drive rated at 0.4 DWPD over five years is designed around approximately 400GB of full-drive-equivalent writes per day on average under the warranty endurance definition.
 That is useful when cache software reports actual daily SSD writes.
 How Much Endurance Does a Home NAS Actually Need?
 Measure before overbuying.
 If your read-write cache receives 100GB of writes per day:

 Even a 600TBW drive has substantial theoretical headroom under that simplified workload.
 If your NAS writes 1TB per day to cache, the calculation changes completely.
 Read Cache Is Much Easier on Endurance
 A read-only cache does not experience the same constant write pressure as write-back caching.
 For read-heavy cache, high endurance is still beneficial but may not justify enterprise pricing if the NAS supports a good consumer SSD and writes are modest.
 Containers and Databases Need Capacity as Well as Endurance
 A 400GB enterprise SSD with PLP may be perfect for cache but too small for:
 Several VM disks.
 Large Docker volumes.
 Immich thumbnails/database.
 Nextcloud application storage.
 AI model/application datasets.
 For those workloads, 2TB or 4TB SN700/990 PRO-class drives may deliver more practical value.
 Mirror Application SSDs Where Uptime Matters
 Two M.2 slots allow a simple mirrored application pool on NAS platforms that support it.

 You lose half the raw capacity but avoid one SSD failure taking every application offline.
 RAID Is Still Not a Backup for SSD Pools
 A mirrored NVMe pool protects against a member failure, not:
 Deleted container volumes.
 Database corruption.
 Ransomware.
 Bad application upgrades.
 NAS failure.
 Back up application configuration and databases to the HDD pool and then protect the NAS itself with independent backups.
 RAM Can Matter More Than the SSD Upgrade
 Containers and VMs require memory as well as storage IOPS.
 If the NAS has only 4GB RAM and constantly swaps or kills services, moving Docker to a faster NVMe drive will not solve the root problem.
 Use How Much RAM Does a NAS Need for Docker, Plex and VMs? before building a large flash application tier.
 Do Not Ignore Firmware and Vendor Lists
 NAS compatibility is more important than a desktop motherboard’s “any NVMe should work” assumption.
 Possible restrictions include:
 Cache only vs storage-pool support.
 Approved SSD lists.
 Maximum capacity.
 Health monitoring availability.
 Firmware-specific support.
 Support/warranty limitations.
 Always verify the exact combination in NAS Drive Compatibility: What to Check on Synology, UGREEN and QNAP .
 Synology Buyers Need to Be Especially Careful
 Synology differentiates SSD cache support and M.2 storage-pool support by model and compatible drive.
 If your goal is a supported M.2 storage pool, check the DSM documentation before assuming a third-party Samsung/WD/Seagate SSD will provide the same supported configuration.
 That can make the higher-cost Synology SNV5420 rational where support certainty matters.
 QNAP Buyers Should Check Onboard vs QM2 Slot Behaviour
 QNAP NAS systems can expose M.2 through onboard slots or QM2 PCIe expansion cards.
 The function, PCIe lane count and storage-pool/cache support can differ by model and adapter.
 Do not buy a high-end SSD before checking the exact hardware path.
 UGREEN / ASUSTOR / TerraMaster Can Be More Flexible, but Still Verify
 These platforms commonly support third-party M.2 SSDs more flexibly than tightly controlled vendor ecosystems, but model-specific lane widths, maximum sizes, heatsinks and storage-pool features still vary.
 Compatibility first, speed second.
 Which Capacity Should You Buy?
 Capacity Best fit 
 240–500GB Read cache, small write cache, OS/app metadata 
 800GB–1TB Cache, small container pool, database pool

 Do not size cache from total HDD capacity. Size it from the hot working set. For storage pools, size from actual application/VM growth plus free-space headroom.
 Best NVMe for Read/Write Cache
 Our preference order is:
 Synology SNV5420 when running supported Synology hardware and support/PLP matter most.
 Kingston DC2000B when hardware PLP and enterprise behaviour matter more than capacity.
 WD Red SN700 when you need a larger, high-endurance NAS SSD.
 IronWolf 525 when your NAS compatibility list favours it or you want Seagate’s NAS-focused Gen4 option.
 Best NVMe for Docker and Containers
 For a persistent application pool:
 WD Red SN700 2TB/4TB: best combination of capacity and NAS endurance.
 Samsung 990 PRO 2TB/4TB: excellent performance/capacity where the platform supports it and PLP is not a requirement.
 IronWolf 525 2TB: strong NAS-focused alternative with high endurance.
 Best NVMe for VMs
 VMs benefit from capacity and random IOPS.
 WD Red SN700 and Samsung 990 PRO are particularly practical because they reach 4TB, allowing a mirrored pair to provide roughly 4TB of protected raw flash capacity before filesystem overhead.
 For business-critical VMs, enterprise PLP may matter more than maximum capacity, pushing the decision toward Synology/Kingston or a purpose-built enterprise platform.
 When a Consumer SSD Is Good Enough
 Container writes are modest.
 The pool is mirrored.
 The NAS is UPS-protected.
 Application data is backed up.
 Endurance monitoring shows plenty of headroom.
 The vendor supports the SSD.
 In that environment, paying enterprise prices purely for PLP can be unnecessary.
 When an Enterprise / NAS SSD Is Worth Paying For
 Write-back cache.
 High daily write volume.
 Critical databases.
 Business workloads.
 Frequent VM writes.
 Vendor-supported Synology storage/cache.
 You specifically require hardware PLP.
 A Practical Buying Matrix
 Scenario Best direction Why

 Small high-integrity cache Kingston DC2000B Hardware PLP + enterprise consistency 
 Large Docker/VM pool SN700 4TB / 990 PRO 4TB High capacity + low latency

 Read-only cache Moderate-endurance compatible NVMe Lower write stress

 Best NVMe SSDs for NAS Cache and Containers: The Bottom Line
 WD Red SN700 is the best general-purpose NAS choice. Its 250GB–4TB range, five-year warranty and up to 5,100TBW endurance make it unusually well suited to both cache and persistent application storage.
 Seagate IronWolf 525 is the strongest direct NAS alternative. It combines PCIe 4.0, high TBW ratings and published sustained-write behaviour rather than relying only on peak burst performance.
 Synology SNV5420 is the compatibility-first choice for supported Synology systems. It adds hardware power-loss protection and enterprise steady-state specifications, and it avoids the uncertainty of unsupported third-party M.2 use.
 Kingston DC2000B is ideal for smaller high-integrity cache/server roles. Its PLP and steady-state orientation matter more than its limited 960GB maximum capacity.
 Samsung 990 PRO is best treated as a high-capacity application/VM SSD rather than our first choice for heavy write-back cache. Its 2TB/4TB capacities and strong random performance make it excellent for containers when the NAS supports it.
 Finally, never shop for a NAS SSD by headline MB/s alone. Check the exact M.2 slot bandwidth, vendor compatibility, supported cache/storage-pool mode, endurance and cooling. A slower-looking NAS SSD that stays cool and survives years of writes is often the better server component.

Best 4-Bay NAS for a Home (2026) 
 As an Amazon Associate we earn from qualifying purchases. Prices and availability come from Amazon.com as of the last update and may change.
 Quick answer
 The 4-bay is the sweet spot of home NAS, and the best all-rounder is the UGREEN DXP4800 (Intel N100) or Synology DS423+ for software polish. If you want power, ECC integrity and an upgrade path, the Synology DS923+ or the 10GbE UGREEN DXP4800 Plus are the pick. Four bays running RAID5 or SHR lose only about a quarter to redundancy, giving the best balance of usable capacity and protection.

 Why 4-bay is the sweet spot
 Four bays is where home NAS makes the most sense. With four drives you can run RAID5 or Synology's SHR, which uses the equivalent of one drive for protection and leaves the other three as usable space. That means you lose only around a quarter of your raw capacity to redundancy, compared with half on a 2-bay mirror, so you get far more storage per pound while still surviving a single drive failure.
 A 4-bay also has the headroom to do everything a home throws at it: back up every device, hold a growing photo and video library, run Plex, and host a small home lab or container or two. The popular Intel models add a graphics engine for hardware transcoding and NVMe slots for caching, which keeps the box responsive as the library grows.
 Crucially, four bays give you room to grow. You can start with two or three drives and add more later, expanding the volume without rebuilding from scratch on platforms that support it.

 Best value all-rounder UGREEN DXP4800 Intel N100, NVMe slots and 2.5GbE handle Plex, backups and apps at a keen price.

 Latest Synology 4-bay Synology DS925+ Ryzen V1500B, ECC and 2.5GbE in the current generation. 
 How much to budget
 Plan the enclosure and drives as a single cost, because four NAS drives can easily cost as much as the box itself, or more at higher capacities. The listed price is for an empty appliance, so add your chosen drives to reach a true figure.
 Fit NAS-rated CMR drives such as Seagate IronWolf, WD Red Plus or Toshiba N300, and consider Seagate Exos for the lowest price per terabyte when you want large capacities. Avoid SMR drives like the old WD Red EFAX in RAID. You can populate all four bays at once or start with two or three and expand later, which spreads the cost.
 Because four-bay arrays lose only about a quarter to redundancy, your money buys more usable space than on a 2-bay. A sensible build with three or four mid-to-high-capacity drives in SHR or RAID5 gives a large, protected pool that should last years.
 Value 4-bay or premium 4-bay
 Choose a value 4-bay (DXP4800, DS423+) if
 You want Plex, backups and photos without overspending
 Gigabit or 2.5GbE networking is fast enough for you
 You do not need ECC memory or 10GbE
 Software polish or hardware value matters more than raw power
 Choose a premium 4-bay (DS923+, DXP4800 Plus) if
 You want ECC memory for data integrity
 You edit large files and want 10GbE off the NAS
 You plan to run heavier apps, VMs or many containers
 You want NVMe pools or cache and room to add memory

 Frequently asked questions
 How much usable space does a 4-bay actually give?
 With RAID5 or SHR using one drive's worth of capacity for protection, four equal drives give you roughly three drives of usable space. So four six-terabyte drives provide about eighteen terabytes usable. That is a much better ratio than a 2-bay mirror, which gives only half.
 Can I add drives to a 4-bay later?
 Yes. You can start with two or three drives and add more as you need them. On Synology SHR and similar systems the volume expands to include the new drive without rebuilding everything, which makes a 4-bay easy to grow into over time.
 Do I need ECC memory in a home 4-bay?
 ECC corrects rare memory errors and adds peace of mind for data integrity, which is why models like the DS923+ and DS925+ include it. For general home use it is a nice-to-have rather than essential, but photographers and small businesses storing irreplaceable data tend to value it.
 Is 10GbE worth it on a 4-bay?
 For most home tasks like backups and streaming, 2.5GbE is plenty and 10GbE is overkill. 10GbE earns its place if you edit large photo or video files directly off the NAS. The DXP4800 Plus builds it in and the DS923+ accepts an optional card.
 What RAID level should I run on four bays?
 RAID5 or SHR is the usual choice: it protects against one drive failing while keeping most of your capacity usable. If you want to survive two simultaneous failures you would need RAID6 or SHR-2, which is more common once you move to five or more bays.

 What is the best NAS in 2026?
 The Synology DS225+ is the best NAS for most people thanks to its polished DSM software, two-bay redundancy and great backup/photo apps. For Plex media the QNAP TS-264 (hardware 4K transcoding) is best, and the Synology DS124 is the best budget entry point.

 These are transitional times for the storage market. After a year of relative price stability, familiar PCIe 4.0 and USB 3.2 drives are starting to creep upward in cost. At the same time, new PCIe 5.0 and USB4 models are landing with more efficient controllers, denser flash, and lower prices than earlier hardware built on the same interfaces. And in the biggest shake-up , Micron has abruptly shuttered its consumer brand, Crucial – a move that could meaningfully hurt competition in the SSD space. 
 Whether you're upgrading a gaming PC, a creative workstation, or a laptop, today's NVMe drives continue to push the boundaries of speed and reliability. For bulk storage needs, traditional hard drives still provide the best cost-per-terabyte, making them ideal for large media libraries and backups. External SSDs, meanwhile, strike a sweet spot between speed and portability, giving you fast access to your files wherever you go.
 As always, TechSpot's top storage picks are organized by form factor and use case, making it easy to zero in on the right option for your specific needs.

 If you want the very best SSD you can buy right now, your two main options are the Sandisk WD Black SN8100 (previously sold under Western Digital's name) and the Crucial T710 (while supplies last). Both drives use the same Silicon Motion controller, paired with different flavors of flash memory.
 While the WD SN8100 usually tops the charts in synthetic benchmarks, the T710 pulls ahead in efficiency. That extra efficiency is why the previous-gen T705's optional heat spreader, shaped like a Mayan pyramid, was retired in favor of something that looks more like a pencil holder.
 If you need 8TB on a single drive, the SanDisk model is the obvious pick. It's a massive step up from the older SN850X in sustained writes and power efficiency, even on systems that only support PCIe 4.0.
 Saving a bit
 The Samsung 9100 Pro is easy to overlook as a 990 Pro with PCIe 5.0 tacked on, but for most people it's more than enough, and with the current price difference it's a worthwhile investment. Even if your current system doesn't support PCIe 5.0, your next one almost certainly will.
 For desktop PCs, we generally recommend an SSD with its own DRAM, which helps when you're digging through hundreds of gigabytes of data. For a laptop, however, this consideration is often secondary to power draw. That's where the SanDisk WD Black SN7100 lands: it's limited to PCIe 4.0, but uses the same flash as the SN8100, making it far more efficient than older PCIe 4.0 options.
 Best for Older PCs and Laptops
 The Samsung 870 Evo remains the only decent SATA SSD on the market. It includes onboard DRAM – critical for SATA drives that can't lean on system memory – and uses TLC flash. If you're upgrading a desktop or laptop that only supports SATA, this is your go-to option.
 Back to top ▵
 Best for Mobile Devices like the Steam Deck and Surface Pro
 Corsair MP600 Mini

 To expand storage on a Steam Deck , Asus ROG Ally , or Surface Pro , you're locked into a single form factor: the short 2230 M.2 drive. Updated in 2024 with Phison's E27T controller, the Corsair MP600 Mini is essentially a fun-sized version of the MP600 Elite, one of the best DRAM-less SSDs of its day.
 To stay Steam Deck-friendly, all components sit on one side of the PCB. That layout forces manufacturers to use denser flash for 2TB models, but in practice it doesn't change much.
 Since the Deck only runs at PCIe 3.0 speeds, you won't see any real-world difference between the MP600 Mini and the older SanDisk WD Black SN770M , which can't take full advantage of its PCIe 4.0 interface anyway.
 There are other 2230 M.2 drives out there, but they either top out at smaller capacities or rely on QLC flash, making them a poor value – if they provide any savings at all.

 Best Portable SSDs

 Fast, portable storage can be a lifesaver in some situations and a routine necessity in others. External drive enclosures let you turn an internal SSD into an external one – and potentially swap it back later – while adding perks like USB4 speeds and water/shock-resistant housings. But if you're shopping for a brand-new drive, today's all-in-one externals offer surprisingly strong value.
 Right now, the standout pick is Corsair's USB4-enabled EX400U , which delivers 4,000 MB/s reads and 3,600 MB/s writes. In long, sustained transfers it's no faster than USB 3.2 options like Samsung's T9 or Crucial's X10 Pro , but it still hits impressive peak speeds. It even supports MagSafe, letting you snap it onto the back of your phone and record video straight to the drive.
 If you have a Thunderbolt 5 connector, LaCie's Rugged Pro5 can push things even further with 6,700 MB/s reads and 5,300 MB/s writes. The catch: it may not work at all on anything slower than USB4.
 It's a solid choice if you just want extra storage on a Mac, but if you plan to shuttle files between different systems, the Corsair drive remains the safer, more compatible option. And if the appeal of the LaCie is its tough exterior, you can always opt for the Rugged SSD4 instead.

 For years, WD Red Plus and Seagate IronWolf drives have been the default picks for secondary PC storage and home NAS setups, while their higher-end siblings – WD Red Pro and IronWolf Pro – target larger, more demanding server environments.
 The catch is that these drives tend to get frequent but silent mid-cycle updates with no name changes, and major outlets rarely review the refreshed versions. In their current iterations, both brands are essentially equivalent: you get a three-year warranty, 256MB of cache, and high-density platters that offset their relatively low spindle speeds, keeping noise levels down.
 Our advice comes down to buying experience: Seagate still sells older models alongside faster and quieter ones, and it's not always easy to tell them apart. WD is more straightforward – you can be fairly certain whether you're getting the latest revisions.
 Budget Option: WD Blue
 If you're just dropping a single drive into your PC and don't need vibration resistance, the WD Blue and Seagate Barracuda are the two mainstream options. WD gets the nod here for a different reason: most current Blue models use conventional magnetic recording (CMR) instead of shingled magnetic recording (SMR), which trades performance for higher density. CMR simply offers more consistent behavior for everyday desktop use.
 Back to top ▵
 Best External Hard Drive

 The cost and capacity advantages of mechanical drives make them a smart pick for storing data outside your PC. Backups, media archives, and other massive datasets – the kind that easily stretch into multiple terabytes – are often safer and more manageable when kept externally. For maximum reliability, your best bet is placing one of our recommended internal HDDs inside an external enclosure with its own power connector. That setup helps ensure a broken USB port won't suddenly lock you out of your files.
 But if you'd rather go the plug-and-play route, WD's My Book is the clear standout, offering a lot of dependable storage for surprisingly little money. Models run from 4TB all the way up to 26TB. Currently, some of the better options are the 8TB model for $170 , the 12TB version for $235 , and the 16TB drive for $300 . 
 The My Book ships pre-formatted in exFAT and includes WD's backup software for Windows and macOS. Just don't expect speed: with a slow-spinning disk drive and a USB 3.0 interface, sequential reads and writes land around 170 – 180 MB/s, with even slower random access. Those numbers would be unacceptable for a boot drive, but they're perfectly fine for the My Book's main purpose: cost-effective, reliable storage for infrequently accessed data.
 There are a few quirks to consider. The drive uses a Micro-B USB 3.0 to USB-A connector instead of the more common USB-C, and it lacks an activity LED. It also relies on a separate 12V power adapter (included), which makes it better suited to a stationary setup. On the upside, you get password-protected 256-bit hardware encryption and a three-year warranty – longer than Seagate's competing model. Overall, the WD My Book remains the best budget-friendly external storage option available today.
 A Compact Alternative: WD My Passport Ultra
 If you want something portable without breaking the bank, WD's My Passport Ultra strikes an ideal balance of capacity, performance, portability, and price.
 Its slim, pocket-ready design houses up to 6TB of storage, though the 5TB model currently offers the best bang for the buck at $125. Smaller 1TB, 2TB, and 4TB versions fill out the lower end. This drive also brings welcome upgrades like a USB-C port (with a USB-A adapter included), an activity light, onboard hardware encryption, useful software tools, and a three-year warranty.
 Performance won't blow you away, but its roughly 130 MB/s read and write speeds are right in line with similar portable HDDs. Considering the price, features, and convenience, that's more than enough for everyday storage needs.
 Back to top ▵

 If you don't have the need for a desktop PC, a pre-built NAS can be a compact and power-efficient alternative for backing up files from all your devices. These days, QNAP seems to offer the best balance of features and ease of use.
 One of the best options is the QNAP TS-464-8G, a four-bay unit that supports SATA HDDs or SSDs in RAID 0, 1, 5, 6, or 10, with up to 72TB of total capacity before you even consider expansion units. It also includes two PCIe 3.0 x1 M.2 slots that can take 2TB SSDs for caching or extra storage – still faster than SATA, no expansion cards required.
 The TS-464-8G runs on Intel's Celeron N5095 and ships with a single 8GB RAM stick (expandable to 16GB). Connectivity is generous: dual 2.5Gb Ethernet ports with trunking, two USB 3.1 ("3.2 Gen 2") ports, and an HDMI 2.1 port capable of 4K60 output.
 For $1,009, you can buy it pre-configured with four 4TB WD Red Plus drives in RAID 5, giving you 12TB of usable space and protection against a single-drive failure.
 Synology Alternatives
 If you have a preference for Synology's NAS models or their software, the DS925+ is a powerful $600 4-bay NAS that supports up to 80TB of raw capacity, plus two NVMe SSDs for cache or storage, and it can scale to a total of nine drives via an expansion unit. 
 Powered by a quad-core AMD Ryzen V1500B, the DS925+ includes 4GB of DDR4 RAM (expandable to 32GB), two 2.5Gb Ethernet ports with link aggregation, a USB-C expansion port, and two USB 3.0 ("3.1 Gen 2") ports.
 For less, Synology's entry-level DiskStation DS225+ is a great two-bay NAS starting at $340. It includes two empty drive bays and two M.2 slots, supporting up to 40TB of total storage. Essentially a refresh of the older DS224+, it features a quad-core Celeron J4125, 2GB of DDR4 RAM (expandable to 6GB), both 2.5Gb and 1Gb LAN ports, and two USB 3.0 ports.
 With only two bays, RAID options include Synology Hybrid RAID, Basic, JBOD, RAID 0, and RAID 1. The one major drawback: there's no support for an expansion unit if you need more storage down the line.

 NAS SSD 2026: SSD Cache or All-Flash NAS?
 By Engin Buldak Published October 28, 2026 Live figures, as of Nov 3, 2026, 7:17 AM UTC 12 min read 
 An SSD in a NAS works either as a cache in front of the hard drives or as the only storage in an all-flash NAS. Synology requires one SSD for a read-only cache and at least two identical SSDs for a read-write cache, and NAS SSDs like the WD Red SN700 or Seagate IronWolf 525 are rated for more writes than many desktop SSDs. On amazon.com, M.2 NVMe SSDs cost $133.85 per TB right now according to the ratioDB TB index (as of Nov 3, 2026 at 7:17 AM UTC).
 This guide explains when an SSD makes your NAS faster, how many SSDs you need and how to tell a suitable drive. We compare NAS SSD lines by TBW (terabytes written, the maximum write volume the maker allows) and show current prices on amazon.com. Which hard drives belong in a NAS is covered in Best NAS hard drive .
 What is the best SSD for a NAS?
 The right NAS SSD has a high TBW rating, a 5 year warranty and the form factor your NAS takes: M.2 NVMe for cache slots, 2.5" SATA for regular drive bays. NAS SSDs like the WD Red SN700 carry a high TBW rating according to their data sheets. 
 A NAS (Network Attached Storage) runs around the clock. SSDs inside it see more writes than in a desktop PC, especially as a write cache. The three ways to use an SSD in a NAS:
 Use How many SSDs Form factor What for 
 Read-only cache at least 1 mostly M.2 NVMe faster reads of frequently used files 
 Read-write cache at least 2 identical mostly M.2 NVMe faster reads and writes of small files 
 All-flash NAS every bay 2.5" SATA or M.2 top speed, smaller capacity 
 The number of SSDs for a cache comes from Synology's SSD cache white paper ( Synology SSD Cache White Paper ). Check your NAS maker's compatibility list before you buy. Especially for M.2 SSDs, some models only accept listed drives for cache or storage pools, and according to NAS Compares that still applies to Synology after the DSM 7.3 update ( NAS Compares, 10/08/2025 ).
 Is an SSD cache worth it on a NAS?
 An SSD cache mainly speeds up many small, randomly placed accesses, as with databases, virtual machines and file servers with many users. For copying large files in one go, Synology says it brings no benefit. 
 Synology writes in its white paper that SSD cache helps where workloads need frequent access to "randomly placed small blocks of data" and does not improve performance for sequential access. Workloads that benefit include SMB file shares, iSCSI, virtualization, databases and mail servers. In Synology's own tests, random read performance rose 30x with SSD cache, according to Synology.
 QNAP describes it in a similar way: an SSD cache instantly boosts random I/O and suits file servers and collaborative online editing ( QNAP ). What that means for you:
 Worth it: several users, virtual machines, Docker containers, databases, lots of small files like photo libraries.
 Barely worth it: streaming movies, big backups in one go, a single user copying large files.
 Network limit: a 1 Gbps network delivers at most 125 MB/s in theory. With large files the network is often the limit, and the cache mostly helps responsiveness.
 Do I need one or two SSDs for a NAS cache?
 For a read-only cache, Synology says one SSD is enough. A read-write cache needs at least two SSDs of the same type running mirrored. If an SSD in a read-write cache fails, Synology warns the cache becomes a high risk zone for your data. 
 With a write cache, new data lands on the SSD first and reaches the hard drives later. That is why the NAS mirrors the write cache across two SSDs (RAID 1). Synology writes that a degraded write cache becomes "a high-risk zone for data storage" and automatically halts all write operations to that cache.
 Cache type SSDs per Synology Risk if an SSD fails For whom 
 Read-only cache 1 low, data stays on the hard drives almost everyone 
 Read-write cache at least 2 identical higher, data lands on the SSD first many small writes 
 For most home users, a read-only cache with one SSD is enough. If you use a write cache, plug the NAS into a UPS (uninterruptible power supply) and choose SSDs with a high TBW rating.
 What is the difference between SSD cache and auto tiering?
 An SSD cache keeps copies of frequently used data on the SSD while the originals stay on the hard drives. With auto tiering, called Qtier at QNAP, the NAS moves the data itself between SSD and hard drive based on how often it is used. 
 QNAP says Qtier automatically moves data to SSDs or hard drives based on access frequency and is typically used for applications with predictable workloads and high storage demands. A cache instead boosts random access right away. The differences according to QNAP:
 Feature SSD cache Qtier (auto tiering) 
 Data on the SSD copies of frequently used data the data itself, moved by usage 
 SSD capacity does not add to storage adds to usable storage 
 QNAP example 5 hard drives plus 2 SSDs in RAID 1 5 hard drives plus 4 SSDs in RAID 5 
 Suited for file servers, collaborative editing predictable workloads, large storage needs 
 According to QNAP, Qtier needs an x86 NAS or a 64-bit ARM NAS with 2 GB of RAM and QTS 4.4.1 or later. QNAP also lets you combine both.
 How much RAM does a NAS SSD cache need?
 According to Synology, every 1 GB of SSD cache needs about 400 KB of system memory, and the NAS uses at most a quarter of its pre-installed memory for it. A NAS with 4 GB of RAM can therefore manage roughly 2.5 TB of cache. 
 The math: 25% of 4 GB is 1 GB, roughly 1,000,000 KB. Divided by 400 KB per GB of cache, that gives roughly 2,500 GB. With 2 GB of RAM it is roughly 1.25 TB. Synology caps NAS models with Alpine processors at 930 GB of cache in total, according to the white paper.
 For you that means a 500 GB or 1 TB SSD is enough as a cache for most home NAS units. Bigger SSDs only help if the NAS has enough memory and your frequently used data really is that large.

 What makes a NAS SSD different from a regular SSD?
 NAS SSDs carry a much higher TBW rating than regular SSDs of the same size, according to their data sheets. The 1 TB WD Red SN700 is rated for 2,000 TB written, the 1 TB Samsung 990 PRO for 600 TB. Both have a 5 year warranty. 
 The specs compared:

 Sources: WD Red SN700 , Seagate IronWolf 525 , Synology SNV3410 and SNV3510 , Samsung 990 PRO with Heatsink . We calculated DWPD from TBW, capacity and the 5 year warranty, Seagate lists the value in its data sheet.
 Synology states its TBW under the enterprise workload from the JEDEC standard JESD219A. According to Synology, the SNV3510 has power loss protection and the SNV3410 does not. Per TB of capacity, the WD Red SN700 allows the most writes in this comparison.
 What do TBW and DWPD mean for a NAS SSD?
 TBW (terabytes written) is the amount of data the maker allows over the warranty period. DWPD (drive writes per day) tells you how often you may fill the whole SSD every day. DWPD equals TBW divided by capacity times 365 times the warranty years. 
 A worked example with the 1 TB WD Red SN700: 2,000 TB divided by (1 TB times 365 times 5) gives 1.10 DWPD. You can write the whole drive just over once a day for 5 years. According to WD, the warranty ends after 5 years or when the TBW limit is reached, whichever comes first.
 A read-only cache is mostly read, so TBW matters less there. For a write cache or an all-flash NAS with lots of changes, TBW matters. How long SSDs last in general and how to read their wear level is covered in SSD lifespan .

 Is an all-flash NAS worth it?
 An all-flash NAS is worth it when speed matters more than capacity, for example video editing over a 10 Gbps network. Per TB it stays much more expensive: on amazon.com, M.2 NVMe SSDs cost about 3.6 times as much per TB as internal 3.5" hard drives. 
 QNAP lists smaller capacity and a higher cost of ownership for an all-SSD NAS, and maximized capacity at minimal cost for a hybrid NAS with hard drives and SSDs. An example with current prices for a NAS with four 4 TB drives:
 Setup Drive Price per drive 4 drives 
 SSDs only Crucial P3 Plus 4 TB $669.45 $2,677.80 
 NAS hard drives WD Red Plus 4 TB $194.99 $779.96 
 The SSD setup costs about 3.4 times as much as the one with NAS hard drives (as of Nov 3, 2026 at 7:17 AM UTC). For most home NAS units, the mix is cheapest: hard drives for capacity, one or two SSDs as a cache for speed. QNAP gives 5 hard drives plus 2 SSDs in RAID 1 as a caching example.
 An all-flash NAS also makes sense if it should be quiet and use little power. QNAP lists no moving parts, shock resistance and lower power use for SSDs. How SSDs and hard drives differ in general is covered in SSD vs HDD .
 M.2 NVMe or 2.5" SATA in a NAS?
 Your NAS decides: most NAS units use M.2 slots for cache, while 2.5" SATA SSDs fit the regular drive bays. NVMe is faster, but over a 1 Gbps network you notice little of it. 
 Some NAS units have M.2 slots on the mainboard, others only through an expansion card. The Synology SNV3410 uses M.2 2280, the SNV3510 the longer M.2 22110 format (22 mm wide, 110 mm long). Check your NAS manual for the supported length. How much faster NVMe is than SATA is covered in NVMe vs SATA .
 Network Theoretical top speed Math 
 1 Gbps 125 MB/s 1,000 Mbps divided by 8 
 2.5 Gbps about 312 MB/s 2,500 Mbps divided by 8 
 10 Gbps 1,250 MB/s 10,000 Mbps divided by 8 
 These are theoretical limits, in practice a little less arrives because of network overhead. If your network is slower than the SSD, the network is the bottleneck.
 How do I set up an SSD cache on a NAS?
 Install the SSD in the M.2 slot or a bay, open your NAS storage manager, create a cache and assign it to a volume. Along the way you choose read-only or read-write. 
 Step by step:
 Check compatibility: Is the SSD on the list for your NAS model?
 Install the SSD: Shut the NAS down, insert the SSD, start the NAS again.
 Create the cache: In Synology DSM or QNAP QTS storage management, create an SSD cache.
 Choose the type: Read-only with one SSD or read-write with two identical SSDs.
 Assign a volume: Attach the cache to the volume holding your frequently used data.
 QNAP says the cache can be launched, stopped or changed while the system is running, without a shutdown. Before removing a write cache, check your NAS help for the safe way to do it, so no data that has not been written yet gets lost.

 What should I look for when buying a NAS SSD?
 Check the compatibility list, form factor, TBW, warranty and price per TB. For a write cache, buy two identical SSDs. Power loss protection, as on the Synology SNV3510, is a plus for a write cache. 
 The key points:
 Compatibility: Is the SSD on your NAS maker's list? Synology says it tests the SNV3000 series for compatibility with its systems after every engineering change.
 Form factor: M.2 2280 or 22110 for cache slots, 2.5" SATA for bays.
 TBW: As high as possible for a write cache, see the comparison above.
 Warranty: NAS SSDs from WD, Seagate and Synology carry 5 years according to their makers.
 Pairs: Two SSDs of the same type for a write cache.
 Price per TB: Small cache SSDs cost more per TB but little in total.
 How does ratioDB compare NAS SSDs?
 ratioDB checks the amazon.com prices of every listed SSD regularly and converts them to price per TB, with 1 TB equal to 1,000,000,000,000 bytes. We recognize NAS SSDs by the line name in the offer title, and the TBW comes from the manufacturer data sheets. 
 The specs come from the linked data sheets from WD, Seagate, Synology and Samsung as well as Synology's white paper and QNAP's page, as of 10/24/2026. We do not run our own measurements. Every offer is listed with condition, price, capacity and timestamp. All rules are on the Methodology page, all offers under SSDs .
 About the author
 I am Engin Buldak and I built ratioDB. I am 37, grew up in Hamburg, Germany, and still live here. Yes, Buldak like the spicy Korean noodles ( ˘▽˘)っ♨ I like my food hot, my storage prices not so much. ratioDB grew out of my own frustration: the well-known comparison sites simply bored me. I am curious, love clear numbers and have little patience for clunky websites. I bring over 20 years of graphic design, programming and SEO, plus a big love for AI. The result compares hard drives, SSDs and RAM by price per TB and GB, with open math.
 NAS SSD FAQ
 Is an SSD worth it in a NAS?
 As a cache it pays off with many small accesses, such as several users, virtual machines or databases. Synology reports 30x faster random reads in its own tests. For streaming and big backups it does little.
 Can I use a regular SSD in a NAS?
 Yes, a regular SSD from a well known brand works for a read-only cache, as long as it is on your NAS compatibility list. For a write cache, an SSD with a high TBW rating is better, such as the WD Red SN700 rated for 2,000 TB at 1 TB according to WD.
 How many SSDs do I need for a NAS cache?
 According to Synology, one SSD for a read-only cache and at least two SSDs of the same type for a read-write cache. The write cache runs mirrored so a failed SSD does not lose data.
 How big should a NAS cache SSD be?
 For most home NAS units, 500 GB to 1 TB is enough. According to Synology, every GB of cache needs about 400 KB of system memory, and the NAS uses at most a quarter of its memory for it.
 How much does a NAS SSD cost?
 On amazon.com, M.2 NVMe SSDs cost $133.85 per TB according to the TB index, 2.5" SATA SSDs $125.47 (as of Nov 3, 2026 at 7:17 AM UTC). A 1 TB cache SSD costs roughly that amount.
 Is an all-SSD NAS better than a hard drive NAS?
 Faster and quieter, yes, but about 3.6 times as expensive per TB as internal 3.5" hard drives on amazon.com. For lots of capacity, hard drives plus an SSD cache are usually cheaper.

 The budget-NAS math changed in 2026 — twice
 The drives. Through 2026, Western Digital and Seagate pointed essentially all of their high-capacity (nearline) hard-drive output at AI and cloud, and consumer NAS drives took the hit. WD CEO Irving Tan told investors the company’s nearline capacity is “fully allocated through calendar year 2026,” with order books not reopening until the first half of 2027 ( winbuzzer.com, 2026-02-18 ; xda-developers.com ). Some NAS-drive SKUs climbed 30–50% off their mid-2025 lows. The two drives in this build are $659.98 of its $1,186.76.
 The RAM. DDR5 memory prices roughly tripled from late 2025 into 2026 as the same AI buildout consumed DRAM output. Chip-level pricing went from about $6.84 per GB in September 2025 to about $27.20 per GB by December — nearly a fourfold jump in one quarter — and consumer module prices followed, with analysts expecting the crunch to run into 2027 ( Tom’s Hardware RAM price index ; Wccftech, memory crisis roundup ). On September 23, 2026 Newegg sold a Corsair Vengeance 16GB DDR5-5600 SO-DIMM for $229.99. The 5825U takes DDR4-3200 instead, and 16GB of that was $93.79 the same day. That $136.20 gap is one more reason this build sits on the 5825U.
 If you are choosing the box rather than the drives, which NAS operating system is still doing the job at month eight is the harder question; the hardware carries the first month.

Both lock you into proprietary software, both charge extra for features that should be free, and both come with a CPU you'd be embarrassed to put in a laptop. For less, the 5825U box with 16GB of RAM and a boot drive costs $526.78, with eight cores and your choice of operating system.
 On the Synology question specifically: the company's 2025 Plus and Value models (DS925+, DS1825+, DS425+) shipped with a drive-compatibility list that threw warnings on third-party Seagate and WD disks and pulled features. Synology reversed course in DSM 7.3 (October 2025) -- third-party drives work again on those 2025 models with full monitoring and alerts, and with every storage feature ( mjtsai.com, 2025-10-09 ). So the drives are not locked today. But Synology framed the reversal as "in the meantime" while it keeps testing additional drives, with no promise that 2026 models stay open. The read: the company walked it back under sales pressure, the lock-in instinct is still there, and building your own box sidesteps the whole question.
 The used enterprise hardware crowd will tell you to grab a retired Dell server. Fine, if you want 120W at idle and a machine that sounds like a hair dryer. The smart budget NAS in 2026 is a small 4-bay box with efficient silicon and an OS matched to your actual needs. Here's how to build one.

The AOOSTAR WTR Pro changed this. Two models, both with 4 SATA bays, dual 2.5GbE, and compact form factors designed specifically for NAS duty.

 Picking Your NAS Operating System
 The hardware is the easy part. The OS decision is where most people get stuck, and the wrong choice can mean a rebuild six months in. All three are legitimate and built for different users; the four-way comparison with Proxmox goes deeper than this section, and the storage-backend guide covers running one inside the other.
 TrueNAS Community Edition — The ZFS Purist
 Price: Free (Community Edition)
 Minimum RAM: 8GB (for up to 8 drives; more is better)
 Filesystem: ZFS (mandatory — it's the entire point)
 ZFS gives you checksums and snapshots, scrubs the pool on a schedule, and is the most reliable storage layer available on consumer hardware. If data integrity is your primary concern — and for a NAS it probably should be — TrueNAS is the safest choice.
 The RAM requirement is real. ZFS uses ARC (Adaptive Replacement Cache) aggressively, and starving it below 8GB leads to poor performance. The old "1GB of RAM per TB of storage" rule overstates it for a home box: 16GB runs this build's 8TB mirror, and a full 4× 8TB array (32TB raw), with a few apps. The 5825U WTR Pro's 64GB ceiling and dual DIMM slots make it the better TrueNAS chassis.
 Community Edition is the Linux line that used to be called SCALE, and its apps run as Docker containers. Version 25.10.7 was the current download on September 23, 2026. The download page also documents the upgrade path from the FreeBSD-based CORE 13.0-U6.8.
 Unraid — The Flexibility Play
 Price: Starter $49 (6 devices) / Unleashed $109 (unlimited) / Lifetime $249
 Minimum RAM: 8GB (16GB+ recommended for VMs)
 Filesystem: XFS per drive, parity-based redundancy
 Unraid takes a fundamentally different approach to storage. Each drive is an independent XFS filesystem, and parity is calculated across drives. The practical advantage: you can mix drive sizes. A 4TB, an 8TB, and a 12TB can all live in the same array as long as the parity drive is the largest. Try that with ZFS or traditional RAID.
 The community app ecosystem is Unraid's real draw. Docker containers and VMs are first-class citizens with a point-and-click interface. Installing Plex, Nextcloud, or Home Assistant is a five-minute affair. For users who want a NAS that does everything and don't want to touch a terminal, Unraid is the most approachable option.
 The cost is real but reasonable. The Starter license at $49 covers 6 storage devices: the four bays and a cache SSD, with one to spare. For a 4-bay build, that's all you need. Unleashed at $109 removes the device limit; Lifetime at $249 also includes lifetime updates.
 The tradeoff versus ZFS: Unraid's parity system is slower for writes (parity calculated in real-time), and it doesn't offer ZFS-level checksumming or self-healing. For most home users serving media and backing up photos, this doesn't matter. For a business storing irreplaceable data, it might.
 OpenMediaVault — The Lean Option
 Price: Free
 Minimum RAM: 1GB (4GB comfortable / 8GB+ recommended)
 Filesystem: ext4, XFS, Btrfs, ZFS (via plugin)
 OMV is Debian with a web UI for NAS management. That's not a criticism — it's the lightest option by a wide margin. If you want a NAS and nothing else, OMV runs on almost nothing. The 1GB minimum is real: it will function on minimal hardware.
 For users who are comfortable in Linux and want a pure NAS without the overhead of TrueNAS or the cost of Unraid, OMV is the right call. It serves SMB and NFS shares, runs rsync jobs and handles basic Docker management. It doesn't try to be a hypervisor or an app platform.
 One important note: OMV is not supported in an LXC container . If you're planning to run it inside Proxmox , it needs a full VM. This matters for homelab users who want to consolidate a NAS into an existing Proxmox node.

 Build a NAS box that exactly fits the role

A DIY case with its own power supply needs sizing for spinning drives; the PSU wattage calculator counts each 3.5-inch drive at its 22W spin-up peak.
 Choose the NAS role before the chassis
 A cheap NAS is only a good value when its storage layout and software match the network and job. For a storage-first home server with two equal drives, start with the TrueNAS mirror build above. TrueNAS’s current hardware guide calls for at least 8GB of memory, a separate SSD boot device and two equal-size devices for one storage pool; this build clears those minimums.
 For an array that will grow one disk at a time or mix capacities, choose Unraid and make the parity disk at least as large as the biggest data disk, as the official array guide requires. For a small Debian-based file server where you are comfortable choosing the storage plugins yourself, use OpenMediaVault.
 Keep adjacent projects out of the base build until the role demands them. A rackmount chassis changes the noise and power plan along with the backplane and controller, so it is outside this compact four-bay brief. An SSD pool, 10GbE link or Plex transcoding box also needs its own workload decision. Use the NAS hard-drive guide for CMR and endurance choices, including warranty, the Plex and Jellyfin NAS guide for media hardware, and the 10GbE guide only after the storage side can outrun 2.5GbE.
 Once the parts are installed, follow the operating system’s own installer and storage-creation documentation rather than treating a buying guide as a setup wizard. Decide the pool or parity layout first, create shares second, then add apps. If Proxmox is part of the plan, use the storage-backend guide before installing either layer; virtualized storage changes which system should own the disks.
 Case, rack and all-flash NAS decisions
 For a DIY NAS case or bare server chassis, count usable drive bays after the motherboard, HBA, power supply and cables are installed. Check motherboard and PSU form factors, cooler height, HBA clearance, drive airflow, rail support and the rack’s usable depth. A hot-swap backplane also needs the right drive interface and enough controller links. TrueNAS’s hardware guide recommends direct disk connections where possible, at least 6Gbps SATA III for hot-swap backplanes, and an HBA or controller in passthrough/JBOD mode rather than hardware RAID.
 A rack NAS pays for density and front-accessible drives with more chassis depth and usually more fan noise. The compact four-bay 5825U build on this page is the fit for a living space or a shallow shelf. Choose rackmount only after measuring the rack and confirming rails, backplane, controller, PSU and acoustics from the exact chassis documentation. That checklist answers “server rack NAS” more reliably than calling one case universally best.
 For an SSD-based NAS, choose media and networking together. The TrueNAS guide notes that flash is much faster and insensitive to vibration, but says to size quality, power-loss safety and write endurance for the workload; NVMe devices can also need dedicated heatsinks. It warns against USB-connected SSDs as primary TrueNAS storage because device serials can be reported inaccurately. Native SATA, U.2 or M.2 bays with adequate cooling are the safer starting point. If the pool can outrun 2.5GbE, plan the 10GbE path at the same time.
 How to use the NAS from Windows, macOS or Linux
 Create the storage pool first, then make a dataset and a user account for the share. For Windows and mixed-device homes, SMB is the usual choice; NFS is the Unix-like option. TrueNAS warns against sharing the root or pool-level dataset, so create a child dataset and set its permissions before starting the SMB service.
 On Windows, enter \\nas-name\share-name in File Explorer or make it persistent with net use Z: \\nas-name\share-name /PERSISTENT:YES . On macOS, use Finder > Go > Connect to Server and enter smb://nas-name . On Linux, install the CIFS client package and mount //nas-name/share-name at a local mount point. TrueNAS documents all three paths in its SMB share guide . Give each person their own account and grant only the datasets they need.

 Do I really need ZFS for a home NAS? For two or more drives storing irreplaceable data — yes. ZFS detects bit rot, scrubs silently, and recovers from drive failure cleanly. Unraid’s parity array is simpler and supports mixed drive sizes but doesn’t checksum data. For one-drive media boxes, ext4 or btrfs is fine. The ‘must I run ZFS’ question really translates to ‘is the data on this NAS worth more than the day of setup time ZFS asks for.’
 TrueNAS vs Unraid vs OpenMediaVault for a budget NAS in 2026? TrueNAS Community Edition 25.10: free, ZFS-native, official Apps catalog, best for storage-first builds. OpenMediaVault 8: free, Debian-based, lightest on RAM (runs on 2–4 GB) — best for small N100/N305 boxes and people comfortable with Linux. None of the three is wrong; they target different priorities.
 How much RAM does TrueNAS need? The classic ‘ZFS needs 1 GB per TB’ rule is misleading in 2026. 16 GB total handles a 4-bay 24–40 TB array running TrueNAS CE 25.10 with a few apps. 8 GB is the floor; below that the Apps catalog gets unstable. 32 GB only matters if you’re running dedup (don’t) or 10+ apps.
 Is 2.5GbE enough for a home NAS in 2026? For a spinning-disk array — yes. A single SATA HDD tops out around 200 MB/s and 2.5GbE delivers about 280 MB/s, so the cable is faster than the disks. The cutover to 10GbE is at the storage media (NVMe or SSD pool), not the workload. See the 10GbE homelab networking guide for when 10G pays off.
 Used Dell / HP / Lenovo mini PC plus USB DAS — is that a real NAS? Yes, with one caveat. The caveat: USB attached storage is not as bulletproof as native SATA/HBA — occasional disconnects happen. For replaceable media, fine. For irreplaceable data, build the inside-the-box path instead. A used mini PC also sidesteps the 2026 RAM spike — you inherit its RAM instead of buying new.
 Why did a budget NAS get more expensive in 2026? Two shortages landed at once, and both trace back to AI data centers. First, Western Digital and Seagate redirected nearly all high-capacity hard-drive output to AI/cloud, and consumer NAS drives climbed 30–50% (WD’s CEO said nearline capacity is ‘fully allocated through calendar year 2026’). Second — the part most 2026 guides miss — DDR5 memory prices roughly tripled from late 2025 into 2026 as AI demand consumed DRAM supply: chip prices went from about $6.84/GB in September 2025 to about $27.20/GB by December, and analysts expect the crunch to last into 2027. On September 23, 2026 Newegg sold a 16GB DDR5-5600 SO-DIMM for $229.99 and a 16GB DDR4-3200 SO-DIMM for $93.79. The 5825U box held at $379. So in 2026 the budget fight is entirely about the two consumables — drives and RAM — not the box. Buy the box new; buy the drives recertified; buy exactly the RAM you need and no more.
